== Biography ==
=== Alexander’s life in its local setting ===

Alexander’s records describe a family rooted in a small part of County Antrim, with children whose later lives lead beyond it. His clearest surviving household is at Lisnagaver in 1851: an Antrim-born farmer, his wife Mary, and three children. Earlier baptisms recover the beginnings of that family; later marriages and the Elder tenancy connect it to the next generation. The probable Gortahar death completes the broad outline, with the last identity link still open.



==== The places in his life ====


Gortereghy<ref name="Evidencec9d92bcd01">[https://www.townlands.ie/en/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin-upper/gortereghy/ Gortereghy].</ref>, written Gortereagh in the baptism transcription, adjoins Lisnagaver<ref name="Evidence7d988f87c8">[https://www.townlands.ie/en/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin/lisnagaver/ Lisnagaver].</ref> to the south. Gortahar<ref name="Evidence10a9c7be48">[https://www.townlands.ie/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin/gortahar/ Gortahar].</ref> lies northeast, beyond Moneyleck. They are distinct townlands within the same parish. The map shows approximate modern townland locations, not reconstructed houses or field boundaries.


Both spouses reported first marriage in 1836. Their children’s baptisms place them at Gortereagh in 1837–38 and Lisnagaver by 1843. That suggests a change in the family’s recorded residence between neighbouring townlands; it does not date a move precisely or establish a return to a paternal home. Mary’s possible local family connections deserve investigation in their own right.


The census’s farmer and literate household, the small assessed tenancy and the children’s marriages recover part of Alexander’s circumstances. Later records call him a labourer, and his son-in-law succeeds him on the holding. These changes are compatible with an altered working role as he aged, but their cause is unknown. No inspected source establishes eviction, poverty, or illness-induced retirement. The record sequence and farm analysis distinguish those observations from assumptions about his life.


The following account traces marriage and children, examines the surviving household, then follows the farm, probable death and paternal connections. Missing parentage is one question within that family history.



=== Marriage, Mary’s family and the children ===

Alexander Glasgow and Mary/Molly McCaughan are a documented couple. Their 1851 household reports first marriage in 1836, but no original marriage entry has been located. Rasharkin Presbyterian’s surviving marriage register begins in 1845; First Kilraughts material (Coleraine Family History Society film 197, marriages from 1831) remains a focused alternative.


The marriage-year statement fits the first directly located record sequence. The published transcription of the original Rasharkin Presbyterian register, PRONI MIC1P/292, records the same parental couple at Gortereagh: James Glascaw was born 17 January and baptised 9 February 1837 to Alex and Mary McAughin; an incomplete 1838 entry records a Glascow child of Alex and Molly McAughern; and a later James Glascow was born 9 October 1843 and baptised 7 January 1844 to Alex and Molly McAughern at Lisnagaver. The named transcription can be checked at Rasharkin Presbyterian baptisms<ref name="Evidence5574dbd555">[https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/Baptisms_1834.html Rasharkin Presbyterian baptisms].</ref>. The register transcription preserves Mary/Molly and McAughin/McAughern. The repeated parental names and residences support their identification with Mary McCaughan while retaining the spellings actually recorded.


The Gortereagh residence is meaningful maternal context, but it is not a parentage proof. The 1834 tithe list includes William and James McCaheran there, a spelling compatible with the recorded McAughin/McAughern/McCaughan forms. This makes a McCaughan family connection a reasonable explanation to test for the newly married couple’s residence, perhaps through Mary's people or a subtenancy. It does not prove that either man was Mary's father, nor that the first son James was named for a maternal grandfather. The 1851 Lisnagaver evidence supplies a more concrete lead: Mary McCaheren, 22, lived with farmer Archibald McCaheren, 60, and Elizabeth in house 31. She is the strongest currently located candidate for the later 1855 bride who named her father as Archy, but that is a separate McCaughan problem. It does not establish Mary Glasgow’s parentage. Likewise, the household of widowed Sarah McCaghrin and grandchildren beside widowed Margaret Elder and children is evidence of a local network of families and neighbours, not an expressed kinship.


The Gortereagh names are recorded in the 1834 Rasharkin tithe book, PRONI '''FIN/5/A/236'''; the 1851 McCaheren and Elder groupings are in Lisnagaver houses 31 and 5. These are separate record observations, not confirmed maternal relatives. See the National Archives census collection<ref name="Evidence0b09d5bb14">[https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/ National Archives census collection].</ref> and PRONI tithe-book guide<ref name="Evidenceb39783b2e9">[https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/tithe-applotment-books PRONI tithe-book guide].</ref>.

An authenticated FamilySearch search adds a useful comparison lead: a John McCaughan marriage at Rasharkin on 18 March 1851 names '''Jas McCaughan''' as his father, while a separate 1836 Lisnagaver valuation entry names '''Archibald Mccaughan Junr'''. The same search returns Archey and John McCaheran in the 1822–1840 tithe collection. These entries strengthen the conclusion that several similarly named families occupied the area, but their original images and townlands still need checking; none currently proves Mary's parents.<ref name="EvidenceFamilySearchMcCaughan">[https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/record/results?count=100&amp;q.anyPlace=Rasharkin&amp;q.surname=McCaughan FamilySearch Rasharkin McCaughan search], accessed 14 September 2026.</ref>

A separate public Geneanet tree repeats the John McCaughern–Sarah Dysart marriage and proposes a 1872 death for John and a daughter, Mary Anne Jane Rea McCaughern, at Crushybracken about 1858. This supplies a useful descendant-search route, but it is user-submitted derivative material and remains a collateral branch, not evidence for Mary's parents.<ref name="EvidenceGeneanetDysart">[https://pt.geneanet.org/fonds/individus/?go=1&amp;niveaux_1___3869569569__=arbres&amp;niveaux_2___3645179592__=arbres%23utilisateur&amp;nom=MCCAUGHERN&amp;sourcename__0__=bobspree Geneanet McCaughern public tree index], accessed 14 September 2026.</ref>

==== What the gaps mean ====


The early children are documented separately from their inferred deaths. The table’s reuse-of-name argument does not supply an exact death date. Nor does the incomplete 1838 transcription identify its child as Samuel: an original copy of '''MIC1P/292, entry 106''' is needed to read the missing name and dates.


The transcription has no entries for 1840 or 1841, around Robert’s likely birth. Failure to find his baptism in that transcription is therefore weak evidence against the known parentage: the census and marriage positively establish his father. The missing original marriage, incomplete baptism entry and missing burial records are different gaps and need different searches.


The unnamed child would have been about twelve or thirteen in 1851. No resident, absent-person or household-death entry records that child in the maintained return audit. That omission weighs against an uncomplicated survival-and-emigration reconstruction, but cannot fix a death date or guarantee that the return was complete. The candidate Samuel Glasgow in Michigan was rejected because no American record supplied the required Antrim/parent bridge and the proposal also had to explain this omission. An impossible February date in a later cemetery transcription cannot name the child. The [[Glasgow-3940|child’s assessment]] preserves the comparison.



=== New parentage research: Mary’s McCaughan/McAughern network ===

The current evidence still does '''not''' prove the parents of [[McCaughan-222|Mary (McCaughan) Glasgow]]. The new research separates several local families that had previously risked being merged by surname and locality alone.

* The complete 1851 Rasharkin-derived return contains several relevant households: the older Archibald McCaheren family at Lisnagaver; William McCaheren; Sarah McCaghrin; Mary McCaheren, age 70, recorded as mother-in-law in the John and Margaret Taylor household; and an 11-year-old John McCaughern recorded as a servant/apprentice. None identifies Mary Glasgow, born about 1811, or names her parents.
* The Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism transcription shows distinct McAughern/McAughin households: Eliza McAughern with Thomas at Carnfinton; Archy McAughern with Elizabeth Kilpatrick at Lisnagaver; and James McAughern, son of John and Jane McAuly, at Ballydonly. These records establish a local network, not a single extended family.
* The 1834 tithe material adds Alexr. McCaughan at Unchenagh in Finvoy, while the Drumadarragh family reconstruction identifies John McCaughey/McCahan, farmer, with children including Jane, Margaret, Nancy, James and Sarah. The Gortereghy William and James McCaheran group remains another candidate cluster. None is linked directly to Mary Glasgow.
* A separate National Archives census-search-form result documents Thomas McCaughern/McCaughan of Gortahar with father John McCaughern and mother Mary Gormley. This is a later-generation, parent-documented local family and does not prove Mary’s parentage.
* Authenticated FamilySearch searches for Mary McCaughan, McAughin, McAughern and McCaheren in the relevant Antrim period returned no indexed result. The apparent Alexander–Mary McCaughan hits belong to a different Catholic Culfeightrin/Ballycastle family, including Mary M’caughan’s 7 April 1867 baptism to Alex M’caughan and Cath Quinn. A separate Mary McCaughern–William Marks cluster is also later and unrelated.

The strongest new route is the pre-1831 '''Kilraughts–Dervock Reformed Presbyterian society material''', PRONI '''CR5/32A/1''' (also appearing in related catalogue references as '''CR5/32/1/1/1–2'''). The PRONI guide describes member-by-society lists, baptisms, marriages, deaths, removals and emigrations from about 1804–1831. Since Mary was probably born about 1811, a household or society entry could name her parents. The Kilraughts and Dervock societies operated together until their 1831 division, so both localities must be searched. This manuscript has not yet been inspected; it is a high-priority evidence target, not proof.

'''Current conclusion:''' Mary’s parents remain unknown. The local McCaughan/McAughern network is now better defined, and the Kilraughts–Dervock family lists are the highest-value unresolved route. No parent should be added to Mary’s profile until an original record explicitly connects her to a named household or parent couple.

Sources: [https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/Baptisms_1834.html Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism transcription]; [https://www.billmacafee.com/182030stithe/tithenorthantrimrevisionorder.pdf North Antrim tithe material]; [https://ulsterlees.azurewebsites.net/families/co-antrim/ballymoney-area/ Ulster Lees Ballymoney-area study]; [https://censussearchforms.nationalarchives.ie/search/cs/results.jsp?applicantAddress=&applicantFirstname=&applicantSurname=&barony=&censusExtractYear=&city=&county=&fatherFirstname=&fatherSurname=&motherFirstname=&motherSurname=&pageSize=10&pager.offset=56160&parish=&search=Search&sort=residence_parishSort&townland= National Archives census-search forms]; [https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/record/results?count=100&q.givenName=Mary&q.surname=McAughern&q.birthLikeDate.from=1780&q.birthLikeDate.to=1840&q.birthLikePlace=Antrim%2C%20Ireland FamilySearch search]; [https://www.americanancestors.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf PRONI Guide to Church Records]; [https://rootsireland.ie/antrimdown/online-sources.php RootsIreland County Antrim source list].

=== 1851 census: the complete household ===

The original return for Lisnagaver house 35<ref name="Evidence96bd10f1c0" /> contains these '''five completed person rows'''. It is the strongest single record of Alexander’s immediate household: relationships, ages, occupation, birthplace, literacy and marriage year appear together. The National Archives catalogue record<ref name="Evidenced9460690a2">[https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/census-record/#census_year=1851&surname__icontains=glasgow&firstname__icontains=alexander&county=Antrim&limit=30&id=43294 National Archives catalogue record].</ref> identifies the return; image reference '''007246523_00175'''.

'''What this establishes.''' Alexander and Mary were recorded as spouses, with Robert, James and Ann as their children, in one Antrim household. It supports the approximate births and reported 1836 marriage year. It does not name Alexander’s parents, or locate every child born to the couple. In particular, Mary’s absence from this return does not outweigh her later father-naming marriage and family evidence.


The remaining person rows are blank. The maintained return audit and the published transcription, page 183<ref name="Evidence26281d6bb1">[https://durrushistory.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/10/1851irishcensusreturnscommadelimitedtextfilejul24_071.pdf published transcription, page 183].</ref> record no absent-person or 1841–51 household-death entry for house 35. That is a statement about this return, not proof that no child or other relative had died. The transcript is another rendering of the same census, not independent corroboration.

=== Following the children into adult life ===


==== Robert: the recorded son and the Scottish continuation ====


Robert, aged ten in 1851, is directly recorded as Alexander and Mary’s son in the same Lisnagaver household. His 5 April 1866 marriage to Jane Graham<ref name="Evidence05c8c53b0b">[https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1866/11531/8240963.pdf 5 April 1866 marriage to Jane Graham].</ref> independently calls him a Lisnagaver farmer and names his father Alexander Glasgow, farmer. Those two records make Robert Glasgow-938 the documented child, with estimated birth about 1840–41 from the census and marriage ages. The often repeated exact 6 November 1840 birth date has no identified supporting original. His probable identification with a later Gortereghy valuation occupier is useful local continuity, but that identification is separate from the proved father–son relationship.


Robert’s later family is followed into Glasgow, Scotland, in the maintained account, which cites a 1871 Scottish census index for Robert<ref name="Evidencea991c3602f">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QV9Y-71S6 1871 Scottish census index for Robert].</ref> and an 1881 index for the younger Alexander<ref name="Evidencecfab144f27">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQQ8-5MB 1881 index for the younger Alexander].</ref>. [[Glasgow-937|Alexander Glasgow (Glasgow-937)]], born about 1871, is the next historical generation in that family reconstruction. The Irish census and marriage provide the direct father–son argument for Alexander-951 and Robert; the Scottish continuation relies here on the maintained census references, not newly inspected original images. The copied exact birth date for the younger Alexander had been cited to the same index used for the census, so it is not adopted as an independently verified birth in this account. Exact Scottish address chronology and Robert’s reported 1902 death remain checks on their own originals.


This carries the story beyond the Antrim farm without making every copied detail equally secure. The tested descendant’s confirmed paternal ancestry reaches Alexander-951; the Y-DNA section explains the genetic comparison without listing living generations.


The precise Scottish birth-image leads and the misplaced 1902 death citation are assessed in the next research tests. Neither has yet been inspected; the direct Irish father–son evidence remains secure.



==== James: a strong Michigan candidate, still an open identity ====


The second James, Glasgow-973, has an unusually clear Irish identity: the 1843–44 baptism and his age seven appearance in the 1851 household establish him as Alexander and Mary’s child. His subsequent association with the James Glasgow buried at Tecumseh, Michigan is strong but still unproved. The Michigan household is well reconstructed: the original 1884 Michigan census image<ref name="Evidence13cf3f6b80">[https://michigan.access.preservica.com/uncategorized/IO_eb4d3f94-3c2f-4701-b5bb-c3ecee9ef9b9/ the original 1884 Michigan census image].</ref> gives a forty-year-old Irish-born baggage agent, and the Brookside register identifies the associated wife and daughters. His daughter Minnie’s 1941 death certificate<ref name="Evidence8b5b1f0905">[https://michigan.access.preservica.com/uncategorized/IO_3dab599e-1093-473c-be85-eee5e9b49154/ 1941 death certificate].</ref> reports James as born in County Antrim. That narrows the comparison materially but names neither Alexander nor Mary and gives no Lisnagaver detail. The 1869 original marriage return, naturalisation papers, or a passenger record is still required before the Michigan life becomes Alexander’s son’s biography.



==== Ann: a later marriage and the Nancy problem ====


Ann, Glasgow-438, is likewise direct family evidence. She was aged four in 1851 and her 13 October 1876 marriage to Robert McCracken<ref name="Evidence157ee58a9a">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1876/11181/8097170.pdf 13 October 1876 marriage to Robert McCracken].</ref> calls her a full-age spinster of Lisnagaver and names Alexander Glasgow, labourer, as father. The occupational wording matters because it independently makes the 1888 Gortahar death’s “labourer” compatible with the former Lisnagaver farmer; it is not grounds to split the two men. Ann’s later married surname also means Nancy Glasgow, who reported Alexander’s 1888 death, cannot simply be equated with her. A separate daughter, or another explanation, remains possible.



==== Mary: the daughter whose records connect the households ====


Mary Glasgow-3167 is not in the 1851 return but is securely added by her 14 June 1871 marriage to Robert Elder<ref name="Evidence5782477e56">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1871/11341/8162804.pdf 14 June 1871 marriage to Robert Elder].</ref>: aged 28, resident Lisnagaver, she named Alexander Glasgow, farmer, as father. Her marriage, Robert Elder’s succession to lot 25, and the Gortahar deaths create the high-confidence bridge between the Lisnagaver couple and Mary McCaughan’s later identity. Mary Glasgow’s 17 February 1892 death return<ref name="Evidence6f1ed437a9">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1892/06049/4723532.pdf 17 February 1892 death return].</ref> records daughter Mary Elder as informant. It does not state a maiden surname or husband, and its reported age 89 conflicts with the retained c.1811 estimate; those limits belong beside the identification, not beneath it.


Mary’s later household also contains an instructive name conflict. Her granddaughter’s 1908 birth<ref name="Evidencebe365902e1">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/birth_returns/births_1908/01647/1657700.pdf 1908 birth].</ref> records '''Samuel Elder''', son of Jane Elder, with no father named; the 1911 household<ref name="Evidenceb4f7bd3ba5">[https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/census-record/#id=490671&c20_year=1911 1911 household].</ref> calls him '''Samuel Glasgow'''. The surname is genuinely present in the census, not merely a modern transcription mistake. These records help reconstruct the continuing family, but neither identifies his father. It would be circular to invent a Glasgow father and then use that invented relationship to strengthen Alexander’s ancestry.


Mary’s absence in 1851 is consequently an unresolved location question within a well-supported later family identification. It does not erase the 1871 father statement. Nor does it establish that she was the Maryan in John of Glenleslie’s household: the roughly nine-year conflict between their implied birth years requires explanation, and no located record joins those two identities.



=== The complete record sequence and the farm ===

The sequence follows the named couple and their children across church, census, land and civil records. A father named on an adult child’s marriage is evidence of parentage; it does not by itself prove that he was alive on the marriage date.

==== The reported 1829 occurrence: an age and identity test ====


The original newspaper alert of '''12 September 2025''' was inspected directly on 13 September 2026. Its MyHeritage result, 12021-100828509<ref name="Evidenceb9eaffcccc">[https://www.myheritage.com/research/record-12021-100828509-/alexander-glasgow-in-united-kingdom-names-stories-in-newspapers-from-oldnewscom MyHeritage result, 12021-100828509].</ref>, does quote '''“Alex. Glasgow, Lisnagaver”''' from the '''Belfast News-Letter, 5 June 1829'''. The British Newspaper Archive issue index<ref name="Evidence2721035739" /> independently locates the Lisnagaver entry in '''page 4, article 015'''. Its OCR mangles Glasgow, explaining why a surname search missed the article while a townland search found it. These are two derivative extracts of one newspaper occurrence, not two independent historical records.


The archive’s damaged heading excerpt appears to concern persons applying to register, with special sessions at Ballymoney, under '''County of Antrim'''. That makes a registration notice the specific working context, but the full image and governing columns remain unread: MyHeritage now presents a subscription paywall and the archive viewer requires sign-in. The extract cannot yet establish an adult qualification, successful registration or the man’s identity. The earlier claim that even the alert was uninspected is superseded; the historical interpretation remains open.

The important distinction is between '''an older birth date for the same man''' and '''a second, older man'''. Even if the notice proves adult status, it would not automatically make the subject Alexander's father. Conversely, identifying the subject from the 1888 age and then using him to validate that same death identification would be circular. No birth estimate or parent ranking changes on the extract alone.


If the subject is Alexander-951, the occurrence would support a premarital Lisnagaver association before the couple's Gortereagh baptisms of 1837–38 and their documented Lisnagaver residence by 1843. That would make a temporary residence near Mary's possible family a more focused hypothesis; it would not prove a move, tenancy or inheritance.


The supplied extract also lists Robert Elder of '''Gortaragh''', Arthur O'Neil of Tehorney, Henry and James Wallace of Culmore, James Tomb of Ballymaconly and James Elder of Drumcon. Their combined names and literal place spellings are useful for locating the correct column despite imperfect OCR. They must not yet be treated as neighbours, fellow freeholders or relatives. The 1829 Robert Elder cannot comfortably be the later son-in-law whose 1871 marriage<ref name="Evidence5782477e56" /> gives age forty and father Nathaniel; the corresponding 1894 death<ref name="Evidencea1cad7ff9e">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1894/05952/4691448.pdf 1894 death].</ref> gives age sixty-four. Those dates place that Robert's birth around 1830–31. A different Elder generation is therefore the appropriate comparison, and '''Gortaragh''' is left unnormalised pending the page.


The next test is the full image of page 4 and the heading governing this entry, with adjoining columns. The earlier PRONI freeholder-search negative does not dispose of this newspaper occurrence. The surname-search failure is now demonstrably an OCR limitation: the exact townland retrieves article 015. Neither search outcomes nor damaged heading text determine the qualification or age of the named man.



==== What the land records can establish ====


Alexander could have been the 1834 occupier at about twenty-three. An older namesake remains possible, but the name alone does not require one. In the 1836 field book, the house section names Robert Glasgow and Archibald McCaughan junior; the land section supplies no occupier names. Alexander’s omission cannot prove he held no land, lived with Robert, or had not yet formed a household.

The 1834 tithe’s Plantation acreage and the valuation’s statute acreage cannot be directly equated to reconstruct an inheritance. The earlier near-equality argument is superseded. Adjoining holdings do not establish three brothers or a particular father.


Robert Elder’s succession to the '''same numbered holding''' is more specific than two surname occurrences in one parish. It supports continuity between Alexander’s family and his daughter’s husband. The immediate lessor was Robert Harvey: this is an estate tenancy, not evidence of freehold ownership. Neither succession nor the annotated revision years prove inheritance or an exact death date. The independent civil records that carry the Elder family to Gortahar are set out once, in the death-identification chain.

Their contribution to Alexander’s family account is explained above; complete household details remain on [[Glasgow-3167|Mary’s page]].




== Research Notes ==
=== Testing the 1888 death identification ===

'''The death at Gortahar on 16 May 1888 remains the best-supported located match for [[Glasgow-951|Alexander Glasgow of Lisnagaver (Glasgow-951)]], but its identification is probable rather than uniquely proved.''' The case rests on a connected family and landholding sequence. The register supplies an exact death date; uncertainty concerns the deceased’s identity, not the precision of that date.



==== The record and its limits ====


Original death entry 348<ref name="Evidencee25dc06500" /> supplies the following details. Nancy’s age and marital status are not recorded; no wife, parent, birthplace or former Lisnagaver address identifies the deceased more narrowly.

==== The identity chain, in dependency order ====


# The 1851 Lisnagaver house-35 return<ref name="Evidence96bd10f1c0" /> establishes Alexander and wife Mary, both reported aged 40, with children Robert, James and Ann. This is the starting household; its identity does not depend on either Gortahar death.
# Mary Glasgow’s 14 June 1871 marriage<ref name="Evidence5782477e56" /> identifies a 28-year-old Lisnagaver spinster, daughter of Alexander Glasgow, farmer, marrying Robert Elder, 40, farmer of Gortereghy. It directly establishes the bride’s father. Linking that father to the established Lisnagaver household uses name, residence and occupation; the marriage does not name her mother.
# PRONI valuation revisions<ref name="Evidence5c88fa9a83" />, VAL/12/B/4/16C–D, follow Alexander’s removal from '''Lisnagaver lot 25''' and Robert Elder’s subsequent occupation. Succession to the particular holding strengthens the identification of Robert with the daughter’s husband. The book neither declares an inheritance nor records Alexander’s destination or exact death. It supplies a separate administrative connection, not another explicit statement of kinship.
# The 16 September 1878 birth of Jane Matilda Elder<ref name="Evidence5aecbbb88b">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/birth_returns/births_1878/02945/2078820.pdf 16 September 1878 birth of Jane Matilda Elder].</ref> places Robert Elder and Mary, maiden surname '''Glass''', at Gortahar. The spelling is retained as written. The parents and later household continuity support identification with the 1871 couple; the shortened surname alone would be insufficient.
# Mary Glasgow’s death on 17 February 1892<ref name="Evidence6f1ed437a9" />, entry 234, records a widow aged 89 at Gortahar, with '''daughter Mary Elder''' present. That named relationship supplies the strongest connection between the elderly Glasgow woman and the Elder family. With the preceding marriage and household evidence, it supports the high-confidence identification of the widow as [[McCaughan-222|Mary McCaughan (McCaughan-222)]]. It does '''not''' name her deceased husband.
# The 1888 death of a married Alexander Glasgow in the same townland fits the husband of that widow. This last step remains inferential: neither death expressly identifies the other deceased as spouse, and Nancy has not yet been connected independently to the Lisnagaver family.


The 1901<ref name="Evidencee493b88786" /> and 1911<ref name="Evidenceb4f7bd3ba5" /> Elder households strengthen the family continuation. They are not independent sightings of Alexander. Likewise, the two civil deaths cannot first be assumed to concern a married couple and then cited as independent proof of that assumption. Their combined value depends on the independently established Elder connection.



==== Ages and occupation: compatibility with genuine conflicts ====

The two death ages describe near-contemporary people, as does the census, and both imply births several years earlier. This parallel is compatible with one elderly couple whose ages were reported differently across records. It does not prove shared identity: the informants may have had incomplete knowledge, the census ages may be inaccurate, or a namesake could be involved. Neither age should silently replace the maintained approximate birth estimate. The paired pattern becomes relevant only after the family connection has been established.


Alexander’s change from farmer to labourer is less problematic. Ann Glasgow’s 13 October 1876 marriage to Robert McCracken<ref name="Evidence157ee58a9a" /> already calls her father Alexander a labourer. Thus the 1888 occupation is compatible with the known father twelve years earlier; it does not require a different man. Conversely, labourer is too common an occupation to identify him by itself.



==== Nancy and the competing Alexander ====


[[Glasgow-438|Nancy’s possible identification with Ann (Glasgow-438)]] remains open. Ann had married in 1876 and would ordinarily appear as McCracken. No inspected record calls her Nancy or places her at Gortahar in 1888. Use of Glasgow does not establish that Nancy was unmarried, but it is a real obstacle to equating the two. Another daughter, absent in 1851 or born later, remains possible; no such birth or relationship should be invented.


[[Glasgow-2385|Alexander of Glenleslie (Glasgow-2385)]] is a genuine competing labourer. His 1847 marriage to Mary Anne Martin<ref name="Evidence4dd66ea875">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1847/09322/5375567.pdf 1847 marriage to Mary Anne Martin].</ref> and 1851 household<ref name="Evidence3f5ed7a43f">[https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/census-record/#id=32216&census_year=1851 1851 household].</ref> distinguish a coherent family with wife Mary Ann and son John. A reported age of 35 in 1851 implies about 72 in 1888, twelve years below the death age. No located record connects this household to Nancy, Gortahar or the Elder succession. He is weaker, not excluded.


The reported 1882 death of his wife is '''unverified'''. Her current [[Martin-93219|WikiTree biography]], checked through the live API, supplies no identifiable original death registration and includes an 1848 Sydney marriage description concerning Mary Ann Cupid. That material cannot establish the Irish wife’s death. Even a verified death would require checking remarriage before using the 1888 married status to exclude her husband.

==== What would change the conclusion? ====


A record linking Nancy to Alexander and Mary of Lisnagaver, or a burial or notice naming the Gortahar man’s wife or former residence, would strengthen the leading identification. A securely identified death of Alexander-951 elsewhere, or an independently documented Glenleslie-to-Gortahar household with daughter Nancy, would challenge it. Tracing the Glenleslie son’s reported 1870 marriage offers a specific next step toward later family residence; that profile-derived lead still needs its original. Present evidence supports retaining '''16 May 1888, Gortahar, probable identification''', with the identity chain and its dependencies visible.


Original excerpts shown here were checked against the saved images. The Mary–Robert Elder 1871 marriage and Mary Glasgow 1892 death remain linked above and supported by the earlier maintained readings; fresh image retrieval returned an access error during this illustration pass, so no new excerpt or fresh reading is claimed for them.



=== Y-DNA: the connection and the competing histories ===

[[Glasgow-951|Alexander Glasgow (Glasgow-951)]] is the project owner’s '''oldest confirmed direct paternal ancestor'''. The documented descent reaches Alexander; his parents remain unknown. A tested male-line descendant has '''Big Y-700 placement R-FT20271''', also found in a tested descendant of [[Glasgow-2738|James J Glasgow (Glasgow-2738)]], born about 1809–10. These are historical ancestors represented by descendant results, not people who were themselves tested. The shared branch establishes paternal genetic kinship between the tested lines. It does not extend either documentary pedigree automatically. FamilyTreeDNA Glasgow project results<ref name="Evidencedb3c53b8e9">[https://www.familytreedna.com/public/Glasgow?iframe=ydna-results-overview FamilyTreeDNA Glasgow project results].</ref>, checked 13 September 2026.


This gives the parentage investigation a concrete family network. Alexander’s connection to James J’s line is established genetically even though the bridge between their families is missing. James J’s proposed father [[Glasgow-2769|Robert Glasgow (Glasgow-2769)]] and proposed earlier connection to [[Glasgow-2304|Archibald Glasgow (Glasgow-2304)]] remain hypotheses. Inserting them into a proved descent would assume the answer. See [[Glasgow-2738|James J’s evidence and open parentage question]].



==== What close STR matching can tell us ====


The maintained comparison gives '''genetic distance three at Y-111''' between the Alexander and James J descendant lines. That makes their connection a valuable research priority. It does not mean three generations: STR changes accumulate unevenly, and observed distance is not the number of father-to-son transmissions. FTDNA’s explanation of genetic distance<ref name="Evidencee3eb9bbee5">[https://blog.familytreedna.com/ftdnatip-report/ FTDNA’s explanation of genetic distance].</ref>.


Another Glasgow line is closer on the larger callable Big Y STR comparison. Consequently James J is the nearest comparison on the specified Y-111 panel, not demonstrably Alexander’s nearest genealogical cousin. The inspected August 2026 Block Tree contains no exclusive named downstream branch joining only these two lines. Wider Y-DNA study and comparison evidence.


Brothers, paternal cousins and descendants of more distant collateral branches remain distinguishable historical hypotheses; the present DNA cannot choose among them. Their similar estimated birth years do not locate their common ancestor. A connection through an earlier generation, followed by migration in one branch, remains compatible with the results. A specific migration route is not established. An exact ancestor, date or cousin degree requires evidence connecting the named people, supported where possible by additional independent descendant comparisons.



==== The SNP evidence matrix ====


The abbreviated branch path is '''R-FT4811 → R-FT32941 → R-FT25406 → R-FT20271''', with FTE32242 downstream. Historical names below label descendant lines, not tested historical people.


'''State key:''' '''D''' = derived, the changed state; '''A''' = ancestral, the pre-mutation state supported by a direct call; '''U''' = unresolved in the reviewed evidence; '''UT''' = untested at SNP level in the supplied comparison. A '''no-call''' means an attempted call was inconclusive and remains unresolved. '''Not independently reviewed''' describes the evidence or pedigree audit, not a genotype. Public source: FamilyTreeDNA Glasgow project<ref name="Evidencedb3c53b8e9" />. Safe study context: Y-DNA research. Private-call results above are a summary of the maintained August audit, not an independently reproducible public genotype dataset.


The maintained pedigree audit places the two FT6135 comparison results through Robert’s sons William and John M, with different confidence in their later continuations. The older James c.1700 label must not be counted as an independent test above Robert.


The FT6135 difference is real in the audited Alexander result and the two supplied comparison results. Its position outside the currently accepted child-branch display makes it a '''candidate grouping signal''', not an established new branch. Resolve FT6135 in both James M son-lines first: derived results would support inheritance at or above Robert under the reported pedigrees and a simple inheritance model; ancestral results would contradict that simple model and require checking pedigrees, recurrence or reversion. Inadequate coverage would leave the issue open. Neither outcome alone identifies Alexander's father.


The two FTE32242-positive son-lines associate that branch with James M's descendants, conditionally on their pedigrees. To locate it below Robert generally requires a reliable ancestral result in a separately documented Robert line. A basal FT20271 label supplies no such result. Missing entries in a variants-only file likewise do not prove ancestral states. FTDNA SNP and match guidance<ref name="Evidence4dd87788ef">[https://help.familytreedna.com/hc/en-us/articles/4402696079887-Big-Y-Matching-Matches-Guide FTDNA SNP and match guidance].</ref>.


For Alexander and James J, compare existing consented calls at named and private variants with coverage and pedigree checks. A shared additional derived state could refine their genetic grouping; it would not make the historical men brothers or identify the mutation's generation. A separately documented Alexander son-line could distinguish variants inherited through Alexander or earlier from changes arising later in one descendant line. STR distance and rounded private-variant averages reuse existing observations: they do not independently date the common ancestor. No narrow common-ancestor date is justified here.


One Robert-associated line and one James M descendant are identical at Y-111 despite different displayed SNP branches. STR similarity therefore cannot recover every branching event. The previous STR reconstruction’s approximate 1750 horizon also reuses marker evidence and has unconstrained dates conflicting with known genealogy; it is not an independent historical date.


The table is available as CSV and JSON, with its dated provenance and unresolved states. A public branch placement can be rechecked at the project; the private-call summary requires the underlying consented files for replication.


The Larne reconstruction connects these genetic comparisons to the actual American and Irish family hypotheses, with each missing generation assessed separately.



=== The wider family: proved links and open bridges ===

The Lisnagaver evidence supports a local Glasgow network; it does not yet yield a single reconstructed pedigree. The starting point is the 1851 sequence. House 34<ref name="Evidence2c97cf113b" /> contains John Glasgow, farmer, with wife Margaret and his unmarried brother Samuel, a linen weaver. House 35<ref name="Evidencedea66e5c28" /> contains Alexander and Mary with their children. House 37<ref name="Evidence6c8cd27a9f" /> contains Thomas Glasgow and Mary Ann. A Watters household separates Alexander and Thomas. The layout establishes a small same-surname farming cluster and useful geographic proximity; enumeration order is not a kinship statement or a property map.


John Glasgow-867 and Samuel Glasgow-2908 belong to a specific '''father-John branch'''. John’s original 16 November 1846 marriage<ref name="Evidencef940c7acb4">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/view/?record_id=cima-3156063 original 16 November 1846 marriage].</ref> names his father as John Glasgow, farmer. The 1851 household expressly calls Samuel John’s brother. That chain directly establishes the brotherhood and names John-867’s father and his occupation. Extending that father statement to Samuel assumes they shared a father; the census does not distinguish full from half brothers. It does '''not''' identify that father with John Glasgow-1022, the older Glenleslie man, and it does not make Alexander another son. The younger John’s memorial says he died in 1895 aged 78, which implies a birth about 1816–17 and makes the candidate Glasgow-1022 less comfortable than an earlier census-age reading alone. Any maintained attachment to John-1022 is an uncertain identification of the father, not an additional record and not evidence for Alexander’s parentage.


The distinction matters because the neighbouring tenancy pattern is tempting but not decisive. The 1834 tithe names Alexander and Robert Glasgow at Lisnagaver, while later valuation lots 24, 25 and 26 are associated with John, Alexander and Thomas under Robert Harvey. Acreage, field-book and adjacency arguments can suggest tenancy succession or a broader network. They cannot establish a biological descent, and Plantation-measure tithe acreage cannot be numerically matched to statute-measure valuation acreage to manufacture an inheritance. The 1836 field book names Robert Glasgow and Archibald McCaughan junior in the house section but does not name Alexander; its land section does not supply occupier names. It therefore cannot decide who lived together, who inherited, or whether Alexander was a brother of John or Thomas.


Thomas Glasgow-987 and Daniel Glasgow-3896 have a stronger relationship argument than Alexander has with either. Daniel’s 1871 will, indexed through the PRONI Wills Calendar<ref name="Evidence968b317eb1">[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/willscalendar_ie/willssearch.aspx PRONI Wills Calendar].</ref>, calls the late Thomas his brother and identifies Daniel Neely Glasgow as nephew; Daniel Neely’s 28 June 1888 marriage<ref name="Evidence47f7d35ebe">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1888/10763/5925382.pdf 28 June 1888 marriage].</ref> in turn names Thomas Glasgow, farmer, as his father. Those two records establish Daniel and Thomas as brothers. Thomas’s PRONI calendar administration<ref name="Evidence9c6dade023">[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/WillsCalendar_IE/WillsSearch.aspx PRONI calendar administration].</ref> adds that the Lisnagaver farmer died 21 June 1870 and administration went to widow Mary Anne on 7 September. It was an intestate administration, not a will, and it names no parent, sibling or heir beyond the widow. It cannot be used to extend the proved brotherhood into a parentage for Alexander.


Alexander may be a brother or cousin of Thomas and Daniel. Shared locality, associated land, church context and descendant testimony make that a worthwhile research model. No confirmed Y-DNA comparison with an independently documented Thomas or Daniel descendant is supplied in this case. None of those sources says that Alexander was their brother, so the three men are not a proved sibling set. The 2020 correspondence records the older Alexander-and-Rosanna belief, but provides no demonstrably independent parentage source: the correspondent said she ''believed'' Thomas’s parents were Alexander and Rosanna, separately wondered whether the user’s Alexander was Thomas’s brother, and supplied neither a record citation nor usable autosomal-match data. The later FamilySearch Pedigree Resource File entries derive from an Ancestry member tree and conflict even on Rosanna’s reported death day. They show the circulation of a tradition, not its verification.



==== The Irish–Canadian family: what the original deeds establish ====


The Canadian connection is now supported by an explicit transaction. In the registered deed of '''30 July 1861''', B465<ref name="Evidence6e02c4a48a">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LWB8-D registered deed of '''30 July 1861''', B465].</ref>, '''Daniel Glasgow of Kilrea, County Londonderry, watchmaker''', and '''Thomas Glasgow, farmer of the County Antrim townland written Lislagaver/Lisnagaver''', sell Samuel Glasgow of Prescott two undivided sixths of the Centre Street property. Their wives are '''Margaret''' and '''Mary Anne''', and the deed expressly derives the interests from Robert Glasgow's will. Place, occupation, wives and the already proved Daniel–Thomas brotherhood identify these men with [[Glasgow-3896|Daniel-3896]] and [[Glasgow-987|Thomas-987]]. This resolves the former uncertainty about whether the will's Irish brothers were the known Kilrea and Lisnagaver men.


Robert's will of '''9 October 1849''', B12<ref name="Evidence8bdc36c751">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LWY9-S will of '''9 October 1849''', B12].</ref>, registered in 1856, gives one sixth each to brothers '''Daniel, Samuel, John and Thomas''', one sixth to sister '''Mary''', and one sixth collectively to '''the children of brother James'''. Combined with B465, this places Daniel and Thomas in the same documented sibling group as [[Glasgow-4010|Samuel of Prescott-4010]] and Robert. The original does '''not''' call James deceased: the earlier death-before-1849 inference is withdrawn. It names no parents.

These deeds concern '''Lot 12 south of Dibble Street and a 3,400-square-foot part of Lot 11''', the house at '''388 Centre Street'''. The municipal designation report<ref name="Evidence4107280a3f">[https://www.prescott.ca/media/3dtiztjk/council-agenda-june-16-2025.pdf municipal designation report].</ref>, printed pp.31–32, and the 2017 property account<ref name="Evidence57849ff728">[https://www.theresataylor.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Auction-all-for-others-Brockville-Recorder.pdf 2017 property account].</ref> agree on 388. The former 280 reference was a project citation error. OnLand's official parcel search<ref name="Evidence43bc477d8f">[https://www.onland.ca/ui/15/property/address OnLand's official parcel search].</ref> identifies PIN '''68159-0153''', Plan 19, Block 2; the historical abstract, p.71<ref name="Evidence675d9ee4bd">[https://www.onland.ca/ui/15/books/48793/viewer/998408458?page=97 historical abstract, p.71].</ref>, connects the same Lot 11 strip to Robert's '''5 April 1841''' purchase from Susannah Jessup. Samuel's '''251 Water Street West''', Plan 19, Block 2, part Lot 16, remains a separate property.



==== James's family: a promising identification with an unresolved title problem ====


Eliza Jane and Mary are explicitly sisters and daughters of '''James the Prescott carpenter'''. Identifying that James with Robert's brother is a strong property-based hypothesis, because both daughters convey interests in the same two parcels to Samuel. It is not yet proved by an express kinship or inheritance clause. Each daughter's '''one-ninth''' interest is also recorded in the official abstract. Together they exceed the '''one-sixth''' collective share given to James's children in Robert's will. Earlier ownership, additional inherited interests or a record error must be examined before treating these as a simple distribution of that sixth. The fractions cannot responsibly supply a child count.


The '''1868 Alexander deed has now been inspected'''. C114, 25 March 1868<ref name="Evidence1f5003a1e5">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LQRC-Y C114, 25 March 1868].</ref>, DGS 008200420, image 120, pp.164–165, identifies '''Alexander Glasco of Rochester, Monroe County, New York, express agent, son of James Glasco formerly of Prescott, carpenter'''. Through attorney Macneil Clarke he conveys '''one eighteenth''' for '''$166.66''' to '''Mary Eno Glasgow, widow of the late Samuel Glasgow'''. The accompanying C113 power of attorney<ref name="Evidenceff75c70d0d">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LQRK-B accompanying C113 power of attorney].</ref> was made at Rochester on '''28 December 1867'''; both instruments were registered on '''18 August 1868'''. The abstract's August date is therefore registration, not the deed's execution date.


This positively identifies a son of James the carpenter alongside Eliza Jane and Mary. It supplies '''three named children''', without claiming a complete family or resolving how their title shares arose. It identifies a Rochester express agent, not a Lisnagaver farmer: linking him to Alexander-951 would require an independent wife, age, birthplace or migration bridge. No such bridge was found in this inspection, so this father statement is not assigned to Alexander-951. The earlier Prescott witness named Alexander is a relevant comparison, but the shared name does not prove he was the express agent either. '''Mary Eno''' is the widow's recorded name; the document does not establish Eno as a maiden surname.



==== Mary Glasgow Black and the Drumoolish connection ====


The original '''C298 deed of 15 September 1869'''<ref name="Evidencea11558442b">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LQTY-K original '''C298 deed of 15 September 1869'''].</ref>, registered '''1 July 1870''', explicitly identifies '''Mary Black, formerly Mary Glasgow, as sister of the late Robert Glasgow of Prescott'''. It names her six children and conveys the family’s interest to Samuel’s widow for '''$800'''. This is another direct Irish bridge: two of the children reside at '''Drumoolish, County Londonderry'''. The deed gives a record-based family to compare with the wider Bann Valley and Inishrush evidence; it does not name Mary’s parents or make her a daughter of Adam.

The six child interests are expressed as '''six sixth-parts of Mary’s one-sixth interest'''; the five surviving siblings also account for Elizabeth’s part. This explains a subdivision within this particular branch. It does not resolve the Rochester daughters’ ninths. Mary Black, Robert’s sister, is distinct from Mary Glasco of Rochester, James the carpenter’s daughter. The deed names '''Mary Eno Glasgow''' as Samuel’s widow, but does not establish Eno as her maiden surname.



==== Consequences for Alexander's parentage ====


The Canadian records now expand '''Daniel and Thomas's documented family''', which makes their brothers' and sister's records directly relevant to this enquiry. They still do not name Daniel or Thomas's parents, and they do not establish Alexander-951 as another brother. The Alexander-and-Rosanna tradition remains a hypothesis about Thomas's parents. Alexander's possible place among James's children now has named family and property records to test, but the carpenter's identity with Robert's brother and any connection between his Rochester son and Alexander-951 must each be demonstrated.


The 1861 deed also places wives '''Margaret''' and '''Mary Anne''' in the recorded family transaction. It strengthens the identification of the existing Irish couples and gives a later dated occurrence of Daniel's wife before his widowed death in 1871. It does not supply either woman's maiden name or establish the mother of every child. No new Y-DNA result was obtained: documentary linkage to the Prescott brothers expands the family that can be compared with Alexander's paternal line, without proving a genetic match or the joining generation.

==== The Black branch and a possible witness at Robert's marriage ====

The original civil return for [[Glasgow-938|Robert Glasgow]] and Jane Graham, 5 April 1866, records Robert's father as Alexander Glasgow, farmer, and names '''John Black''' as a witness. The return gives John no address or relationship. A plausible candidate is the John Black of Drumoolish who married Martha Savage on 13 March 1862, son of Robert Black, farmer; this remains a hypothesis, not a profile identification.

The 1862 marriage return<ref name="EvidenceBlackSavage1862">[https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1862/10945/5491449.pdf John Black–Martha Savage marriage return], page 178, entry 136, image 5491449.</ref> gives John as a full-age bachelor, farmer of Drumoolish, son of Robert Black; Martha was daughter of William Savage. Churchtown's baptism transcription records Elizabeth Black on 31 July 1845, daughter of '''Robert Black and Mary Glasgow''', resident Drumoolish<ref name="EvidenceBlackElizabeth1845">[https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/TamlaghtP/Baptisms.html Churchtown baptism transcription], page 7, entry 116.</ref>. This supplies a named parental couple for the Black branch and makes the deed-based John a specific person to investigate. It does not name Alexander's parents.

The 1831 Tamlaght O'Crilly census transcription lists Robert Black at Drumolish, house 57, with two males and one female, but the occupants are unnamed and other Black households occur in the same townland<ref name="EvidenceBlack1831">[https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/Tamlaght/1831census_2.html 1831 census transcription], row 643.</ref>. The December 1862 report of twins born to John's wife at her father William Savage's home and the 5 November 1863 Churchtown baptisms of Robert and William Black, children of John and Martha, support the couple's continuity<ref name="EvidenceBlackChildren">[https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/TamlaghtP/Baptisms2.html Churchtown baptism transcription].</ref>. The newspaper's 20 December birth and the baptism transcription's nine-month age conflict; both remain reported rather than reconciled.

The 1866 witness fact is established, but identifying him with this John Black remains unproved. Shared congregation and local geography could explain contact without kinship. Even a confirmed identification would not prove that Alexander and Mary Glasgow belonged to the same parental couple. The Elizabeth and 1843 baptism images, Robert Black and Mary Glasgow's marriage, and further Churchtown witness occurrences are the next discriminating checks. The 1843 transcription's “Thomson Black” and illegible mother reading must not be changed to “Thomasina” or “Gear” without the original image.

==== Concrete connections to other Glasgows ====

On 18 February 1875 at Finvoy Parish Church, [[Glasgow-1371|Ann Glasgow]], daughter of [[Glasgow-867|John Glasgow]], married Francis Bellingham. The witnesses were Thomas Bellingham and '''Mary Anne M‘Caughern'''.<ref name="Bellingham1875">[[https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/McCaughan-222#_note-BellinghamGlasgow1875 WikiTree source note for the 1875 Bellingham–Glasgow marriage].</ref>

This is a useful record-level link between John's Glasgow family and a McCaughern surname form. The witness is unidentified and must not be equated with [[McCaughan-222|Mary/Molly Glasgow]]: the record says Mary Anne, uses M‘Caughern, and does not establish that Alexander's wife was living in 1875. It is a network observation, not proof that [[Glasgow-867|John]] and [[Glasgow-951|Alexander]] were related.



==== 1892 New York probate citation: Nancy Glasgow's next of kin ====

The most informative parentage evidence located so far is not an Irish record but a legal notice published in New York. On 14 January 1892 the Clinton County Surrogate issued a citation on the petition of Hiram Walworth to prove the will of '''[[Glasgow-4070|Nancy Glasgow]]''' of Plattsburgh, an unmarried Irish-born woman who had described herself in January 1889 as "about 68 years" old.<ref name="NancyWill1889">Clinton County, New York, Surrogate's Court, ''Records of wills, 1807–1902'', vol. Q, pp. 255–259, will of Nancy Glasgow of Plattsburgh dated 15 January 1889, admitted 9 May 1892; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:33SQ-GYC4-66V?view=fullText FamilySearch image 159].</ref><ref name="NancyCitation1892">''The Plattsburgh Sentinel'' (Plattsburgh, New York), 26 February 1892, p. 6, legal notices, citation in the estate of Nancy Glasgow, deceased, dated 14 January 1892; [https://www.nyshistoricnewspapers.org/?a=d&d=plts18920226-01.1.6 New York State Historic Newspapers].</ref> The notice addresses heirs, next of kin and legatees. Its reference to both real and personal estate matters: the old restriction on collateral representation in personal property cannot by itself determine every relative's standing in this proceeding.<ref name="DeVoe1905">''Matter of De Voe'', 107 A.D. 245 (N.Y. App. Div. 1905), discussion of pre-1898 personal-property representation and the different treatment of real property; [https://law.justia.com/cases/new-york/appellate-division/1905/107-ad-245.html published judicial opinion]. This later case explains the distinction; it is not a decree concerning Nancy's family.</ref>

The citation names no brother or sister directly. It lists only children of named people: '''James G. Glasgow, Ann and Lizzie''', children of John Glasgow, late of "Baladonly" (Ballydonnelly, Rasharkin parish); '''James Glasgow, Mary and Ann''', children of Alexander Glasgow, formerly of Rasharkin; '''Mary Jane and Ann''', children of Robert Glasgow; the Dysart children of '''[[Glasglow-11|Jane (Glasgow) Dysart]]''' in Rasharkin, Ballymena, New Zealand and West Troy; '''David, James and Samuel Anderson of Gortahar''', identified through separate household records as sons of '''[[Glasgow-4071|Elizabeth (Glasgow) Anderson]]'''; and the unnamed children of '''Ann McClelland''' and '''Mary Thompson'''.<ref name="NancyCitation1892" /> Nancy's will independently calls Margaret (Dysart) Kennedy her niece and Robert Anderson her nephew,<ref name="NancyWill1889" /> and the Rasharkin Presbyterian register records both as children of Glasgow mothers — Jane Glascaw at Granagh and Betty Glascaw at Drumack.<ref name="Evidence5574dbd555" /> Together these records support a probable network of deceased sibling branches: John, Alexander, Robert, Jane, Elizabeth, Ann and Mary. Elizabeth is identified through the baptism and household records, not named as a parent in the notice. The list's completeness and each person's exact relationship remain to be checked in the underlying petition.

The Alexander of this citation is probably Alexander of Lisnagaver. His daughters' marriages of 1871 and 1876 each name Alexander Glasgow of Lisnagaver as father, his son James was baptised at Lisnagaver in 1843, and he died in May 1888 — "formerly of Rasharkin" in the citation's language. Nancy, born about 1820–21, was roughly ten years his junior: probable sisterhood fits these ages; daughterhood does not. He spent his last years at '''Gortahar''', where the citation places his sister Elizabeth's Anderson sons in 1892. His son [[Glasgow-938|Robert]] is not named. The proposed Scottish continuity and alleged survival to 1902 need original-record verification; this potential omission prevents treating completeness as already demonstrated.

The John of the citation is probably '''[[Glasgow-867|John Glasgow of Lisnagaver]]'''; Lizzie and the Ballydonnelly residence remain identity checks. His documented children were Ann (born 1848; married Bellingham in 1875, naming father John) and '''James Garvin Glasgow''' — the "James G." of the notice; the "Lizzie" of the notice is an otherwise unrecorded daughter (the Elizabeth Ann on the family memorial, died 1933, was James Garvin's widow).<ref name="Evidencef940c7acb4" /> A John Glasgow of Lisnagaver died on 24 June 1885 with son James as informant, which agrees with "late of".<ref name="JohnDeath1885">General Register Office of Ireland, civil death return, Ballymoney superintendent registrar's district, Dirraw district, entry 2: John Glasgow, Lisnagaver, 24 June 1885; [https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1885/06280/4799372.pdf register image].</ref> John's original 1846 marriage return names his father as '''John Glasgow, farmer''', and the 1851 census makes Samuel Glasgow, born in County Londonderry about 1790, John's brother.<ref name="Evidencef940c7acb4" /> If Alexander and John shared a father, that father would be John Glasgow, farmer. Probable siblinghood alone does not distinguish a shared father from a shared mother or more complex half relationships.

The same document tells against the alternatives. '''[[Glasgow-987|Thomas Glasgow]]''' of Lisnagaver, whom earlier research treated as Alexander's possible brother, died in 1870 leaving children who were adults at Lisnagaver in the 1880s; had he been Nancy's brother they would have been her next of kin, yet none is cited while nieces in New Zealand are. This omission weighs against a simple reconstruction only if expected inclusion and completeness are established. It does not exclude Thomas or his proved brother [[Glasgow-3896|Daniel]] as Alexander's brothers or collateral relatives: Alexander could also share a parent with Thomas without Thomas being Nancy's sibling. The tradition naming [[Glasgow-3904|an older Alexander]] and Rosanna concerns Thomas; its extension to Alexander of Lisnagaver remains unproved. Likewise no member of the Glenleslie family of [[Glasgow-1367|Robert Glasgow]] and Catherine, previously attached as Alexander's parents, appears among Nancy's next of kin; [[Glasgow-1049|Robert of Doonbought]]'s daughters were Catherine, Margaret, Maria, Netta and Jane, not the Mary Jane and Ann of the citation. The Robert of the citation is more likely the second Lisnagaver tithe occupier of 1834 — 35 acres entered immediately after Alexander's 29 — and perhaps the Robert Glasgow of Gortereghy in Griffith's Valuation who died in Ballymoney district in 1868 aged 71; his daughters have not yet been found.<ref name="Evidenceb707c32b1e" /><ref name="GriffithRasharkin">[https://www.failteromhat.com/griffiths/antrim/rasharkin.htm Griffith's Valuation, Rasharkin parish], Glasgow occupiers at Lisnagaver (Alexander, John, Thomas), Gortereghy (Daniel, Robert) and Dromore (James).</ref><ref name="Evidenced078ae5073" />

The reconstructed family of John Glasgow, farmer, runs from Samuel (about 1790, County Londonderry) through Robert (about 1797), John (about 1801, County Antrim), Jane (about 1804), Alexander (about 1811), Elizabeth (by about 1816), Ann and Mary, to Nancy (about 1820–21) — a span that warrants checking estimated ages, identities and possible multiple unions; it does not establish two marriages of a particular parent. If these identities and a shared household are correct, their different birth counties suggest a possible movement from County Londonderry to Rasharkin parish; the John Glasgow recorded as a Desertoghill flax grower in 1796 ([[Glasgow-4090|Glasgow-4090]]) is a plausible but unproved identity for the father, and John of Lisnagaver later married a Desertoghill woman at Garvagh. No record yet names Alexander's father in his own right, and the citation cannot distinguish full from half siblings. The decisive record is Nancy's underlying Clinton County probate petition, which should state each cited person's relationship to her.

Sources: ''The Plattsburgh Sentinel'', 26 February 1892, p. 6; Clinton County Will Book Q, pp. 255–259; Rasharkin Presbyterian baptisms, entries 04, 63, 82, 133, 176, 271; John Glasgow–Margaret Garvin marriage, 16 November 1846; 1851 census, Lisnagaver house 34; civil death of John Glasgow, Lisnagaver, 24 June 1885; Griffith's Valuation, Rasharkin; 1834 Rasharkin tithe applotment, Lisnagaver.


==== Separate Canadian estate leads ====


The bare estate index<ref name="Evidence886dbd1025">[https://www.ontariogenealogy.com/uppercanadaontariopioneerwillsestatefiles/leedsgrenvillecountieswillssurrogaterecords/leedsgrenvillecountieswillestateindex.html bare estate index].</ref> entries '''Samuel Glasgow, 1875''' and '''James E., 1900–09''' remain unassigned. [[Glasgow-4021|Younger Samuel-4021]], two at his next birthday in the 1851 household, is an alternative to the merchant; [[Glasgow-4017|James E.-4017]], five at his next birthday, is a specific comparison for the later James E. entry. These are separate from James the carpenter and the Centre Street deeds.


The 1851 Prescott census<ref name="Evidence9d10d7d2c7">[https://central.bac-lac.gc.ca/.item/?app=Census1851&op=img&id=e002351566 1851 Prescott census].</ref> contains '''eight household members, six probable children'''. With two later sons reported by local history, eight possible children are accounted for, leaving two of the reported ten unaccounted for by those sources. Library and Archives Canada fonds R6229-0-0-E / MG24-I39<ref name="Evidence3488d83655">[https://recherche-collection-search.bac-lac.gc.ca/eng/home/record?IdNumber=98738&app=fonandcol Library and Archives Canada fonds R6229-0-0-E / MG24-I39].</ref> concerns a Niagara farmer who died about 1830 and is excluded as this merchant's archive.


The remaining distinct family groups are Alexander's household; John-867 and Samuel-2908's father-John branch; and the now connected '''Kilrea–Lisnagaver–Prescott sibling group'''. No record yet joins them under a common parent. The new Irish bridge is established; Alexander's position within that wider family remains the question.


The 2020 correspondent identified a descent through Catherine, described as Thomas and Mary Ann’s sixth daughter, and reported an autosomal match. The supplied message contains no shared-cM total, segment information, checked descent or source for the parent names. Her belief about Thomas’s parents and her separate question about Alexander’s brotherhood are two claims that require separate tests. The reported match is a lead to evaluate for other shared ancestral routes as well as this paternal hypothesis. The correspondence is summarised without publishing the private message or correspondent’s identity.



=== The Larne connection: a working family reconstruction ===

'''The Larne–Kilwaughter family is a priority origin hypothesis for Alexander's paternal line.''' The useful model connects an Irish branch with a branch that moved to South Carolina in the 1770s. [[Glasgow-2769|Robert of Tennessee]], born in South Carolina about 1790–94, is proposed as [[Glasgow-2738|James J's]] father. He is not proposed as the father of Alexander, Thomas or Daniel. Their ages therefore supply no objection to that American parentage.


There are two questions to solve together: which older Larne household supplied the Irish branch, and which man in that branch fathered Alexander. [[Glasgow-1509|James Glasgow of Larne (Glasgow-1509)]], reportedly born in 1737, is a concrete candidate for the earlier generation. Identifying him with [[Glasgow-3905|Glasgow-3905]] means testing whether he was '''Adam of Inishrush's father''': 3905 represents that unidentified parental role, rather than a second man established by records. Its placeholder status neither supports nor disqualifies James.

The age fit is stronger when calculated properly. Robert's 1820 and 1840 brackets, combined with Archibald's under-ten boy in 1800, allow '''5 August 1790–7 August 1794''', if all three returns concern him and their age bands are accurate. His 1850 age of sixty requires a modest discrepancy; it favours the older end of the working range. That older end also gives a more comfortable fatherhood age for James J around 1809/10. Her age is a constraint to check, not a general exclusion of the family. Census dates: 1800<ref name="Evidence023fccd184">[https://www.archives.gov/research/census/1800 Census dates: 1800].</ref>, 1820<ref name="Evidence4b42eb2ce0">[https://www.archives.gov/research/census/1820 1820].</ref>, 1840<ref name="Evidenceb15556cf00">[https://www.archives.gov/research/census/1840 1840].</ref>.


This makes Archibald a worthwhile leading named candidate for '''Robert's''' father. It does not make Robert the uniquely established father of '''James J'''. [[Glasgow-2439|James Glasgow (2439)]], born about 1787, and Sarah form another age-compatible Newberry household. Its 1831 estate should be compared with Archibald's. Robert's Bradshaw Creek associates and James J's district-six land trail still need joining. The 1848 deed<ref name="Evidenceeb34fedf89">[https://tngenweb.org/giles/deed-noah-hancock-to-james-glasgow/ 1848 deed].</ref> proves James's residence then; its recital of an 1845 title bond proves the earlier transaction, not necessarily residence in 1845.



==== James of Larne fits the missing older generation ====

It supports the older James identity, although the especially good generational fit below depends on his reported 1737 birth.

| [[Glasgow-3904|Older Alexander (3904)]], estimated about 1770 || 33 || A coherent possible brother of Adam. His own existence and family are reconstructed principally from the later Thomas-parent tradition; no record names James as his father.
|-
| [[Glasgow-3986|Younger James of Larne (3986)]], about 1773 || 36 || An already identified possible son, associated with the 1795 merchant and 1797 junior records. He supplies an alternative route to Alexander's generation without inventing another unnamed James.
|-
| [[Glasgow-1367|Robert of Glenleslie (1367)]], about 1779 || 42 || Fits chronologically as another possible child in the broader reconstruction. No record makes him James's son, and he is not securely identified with the Lisnagaver tithe occupier.
|}


'''The 1762 marriage is the main household condition.''' It postdates Adam's estimated birth by about four years. If James fathered Adam, Adam could belong to an earlier relationship, a premarital birth, or a chronology needing correction. None is established. Janet Shutter must not acquire maternity merely because she was James's later reported wife. The original marriage and earlier Belfast records could distinguish these possibilities.


Nor does James have to move to Inishrush himself. His 1768 sale<ref name="Evidence2f70b79715">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJW-DDXW 1768 sale].</ref> transferred the ropewalk interest, but Holmes's 1799 will<ref name="Evidence0b4b961c56">[https://holmes-history.com/antrim/ Holmes's 1799 will].</ref> still names a James Glasgow, roper, in Larne. An adult son could have moved independently. The ropemaker, the younger [[Glasgow-3991|tanner James (3991)]], and the younger merchant must remain distinct record groups; selling a workshop is not evidence of a family migration by itself.



==== Two routes to Alexander deserve explicit comparison ====



{| class="wikitable" style="width:100%; background:#f5f8f1;"
|-
! style="background:#dce8d5;" | Working reconstruction !! Why it fits !! What would distinguish it

It is much cleaner chronologically than making older Alexander a son of Adam and Rose. || A record linking older Alexander to the Larne family, and an independent record or family register joining younger Alexander to Thomas and Daniel. Alexander's use of James for his sons is compatible with this route. It uses a known candidate of the appropriate generation. || Larne succession records naming James's children, or a Lisnagaver record naming Alexander's father James. The first route better preserves the existing Thomas-family testimony; the second tests the documented merchant and junior occurrences provisionally identified with younger James-3986. Neither has a father statement for Alexander. These are '''competing explanations worth testing''', not equal-probability trees. The local Robert and father-John possibilities remain in the immediate-parent comparison; a Larne origin could ultimately run through either of them.


The earlier Adam → older Alexander route compresses the generations: Adam born about 1758 would be twelve at the older Alexander's estimated 1770 birth, while Rose born about 1767 would be three. Moving the older Alexander's birth later and proposing an earlier mother can make Adam's paternity biologically possible, but adds conditions unsupported by records. A brother or cousin relationship is the more natural version to investigate. This chronological preference does not itself prove their kinship.



==== Where the DNA and the wider catalogue narrow the search ====


The DNA evidence is positive family evidence. Alexander's established descendant line and James J's line share '''R-FT20271''', are three steps apart at Y-111 and share DYS714=27. Alongside James J's South Carolina origin and the documented Kilwaughter emigrant family, that makes the Larne connection worth pursuing ahead of an arbitrary same-surname pedigree. The American household evidence was not derived from the DNA, so their agreement is meaningful. But the proposed links from James J to Robert and Archibald are the very links being tested: they cannot also be counted as an independent proof that the match descends from Archibald.


There are already '''two additional historical comparison routes''' in the public project<ref name="Evidencedb3c53b8e9" />: a reported Robert-1143 line tested at Y-111, and a reported John-822 line tested at Y-67. They place the Larne and Inishrush questions within the same broader STR research network. Their public broad haplogroup labels do not yet establish either as FT20271-positive. Auditing those descent paths and obtaining resolved SNP states would test the proposed geographic connection more directly than treating all current FT20271 matches as interchangeable. John's omission of Alexander from his family Bible weakens '''John as Alexander's father''', not John as a collateral relative.


The proposed older Larne tree must also be tested. James-1509’s imported and live attachment is to [[Glasgow-1505|William-1505]], while the reviewed catalogue also carries a competing Hugh hypothesis. A William Glasgow, merchant of Larne, witnessed the 1760 lease; his identification with William-1505 needs checking against the other adult Williams. The derivative 1737 baptism names Hugh. [[Glasgow-1503|Hugh-1503's]] monument names a different adult son James, born about 1747/48. Both cannot casually be treated as the same child; identifying both as surviving sons of one Hugh would need explanation. William and Hugh's 1736 joint tenancy establishes association, while the proposed connections from them and Robert-1143 to [[Glasgow-1502|Robert-1502]] remain unproved. This is the unsettled joining generation, rather than a reason to disregard the well-supported branches below it.


A second origin model remains useful: the two '''Hugh Glasgow householders recorded in Tamlaght O'Crilly in 1740''', followed by a parish Hugh in 1772, could represent local continuity behind Adam. John's Bible<ref name="Evidence5dc7ff7638">[https://www.hiltner.com/mckeown/getperson.php?personID=I368&tree=tree1 Bible].</ref> gives sons Adam–James–John and second daughter Maria, suggesting older Adam and Maria under a conventional naming pattern. That pattern is not fully followed, and applying it to Adam-3902 depends on the unproved brotherhood. These are substantive local alternatives. They prevent treating a good Larne reconstruction as already the only surviving family.


'''The research can now be narrower:''' test Archibald's missing adult son in estate '''647'''; test the Larne household through William-3324's surviving '''1815 will, D300/1/5/49''', the '''1762 marriage''' and earlier Belfast records; identify Alexander's immediate family in '''CR5/32/1/1/1–2'''; and resolve the DNA placement of the specific Larne and Inishrush comparison lines. Each addresses a particular missing connection. The research priorities explain the outcomes to look for.



=== Alexander’s immediate parents: the remaining comparisons ===

'''Three local explanations addressed Alexander’s immediate parents; since Nancy Glasgow's 1892 next-of-kin citation was read as a legal document, one of them leads.''' The father-John model — the John Glasgow, farmer, named in [[Glasgow-867|John of Lisnagaver]]'s 1846 marriage — is now the leading hypothesis, because the citation places Alexander's children and John's children in the same class of Nancy's next of kin. The older-Alexander-and-Rosanna couple, which reached Alexander through proposed brotherhood with [[Glasgow-987|Thomas]], remains unproved; omission of Thomas's children does not categorically disprove it. The table below records the earlier state of the comparison; the probate-citation section above gives the current reasoning.
